summary: Provides Path Computation Element Communication Protocol extensions for stateful PCE to support point-to-multipoint TE LSPs. The PCE is an appropriate technology for computing such paths. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8623 lets a central path computer manage trees of MPLS paths, not just single paths. It adds the signalling a stateful path computer needs to learn about a tree, change one branch of it, create it on demand and take it away. Because a tree has many branches, the messages name the tree with an identifier and carry only what changed.

questions: what is stateful pce for p2mp
what are pcep p2mp capability flags
subtitle: How a central path computer can build and manage one-to-many MPLS tunnels over PCEP.

tldr.problem: PCEP already let a stateful Path Computation Element manage point-to-point tunnels, but a point-to-multipoint tree has many leaves, so messages are large and changes to one leaf should not require resending the whole tree.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8623 adds capability flags, a P2MP flag in the LSP object, a P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV, a new S2LS object and message fragmentation, and reuses the PCRpt, PCUpd, PCReq, PCRep and PCInitiate messages for trees.
tldr.outcome: A stateful PCE can create, update, report on, grow, prune and delete P2MP TE LSPs, referring to each tree by its PLSP-ID. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 9756 updates it.

today: RFC 8623 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) is an entity that computes a network path or route from a network graph while applying computational constraints, and a Path Computation Client (PCC) may ask it for paths. RFC 4875 describes how to set up point-to-multipoint (P2MP) Traffic Engineering label switched paths in MPLS and GMPLS networks, and RFC 5671 examines the applicability of a PCE to computing paths for P2MP TE LSPs.

PCEP is the protocol between PCCs and PCEs, and RFC 5440 defines it for point-to-point path computation. The extensions that request path computation for P2MP TE LSPs are described in RFC 8306.

Stateful PCEs are shown to be helpful in many scenarios, in both MPLS and GMPLS networks, and those scenarios apply equally to point-to-point and point-to-multipoint TE LSPs. RFC 8231 provides the fundamental PCEP extensions that a stateful PCE needs for general point-to-point operation, and RFC 8281 adds the extensions for a stateful PCE to initiate point-to-point LSPs. This document complements that work with the extensions needed for a stateful PCE to support P2MP TE LSPs, and it describes the setup, maintenance and teardown of PCE-initiated P2MP LSPs under the stateful PCE model.
sections.plainLanguage: A path computation element works out routes on request, and a client asks it for them. PCEP is the protocol they use. The protocol already handles one path at a time, and other documents extend it to trees of paths. This RFC adds what a stateful path computer needs so that it can keep track of trees, not just single paths.

sections.title: Why a Stateful Path Computer Helps with Trees
sections.content:
RFC 8051 presents use cases that benefit from a stateful PCE, including optimization and recovery, and they apply just as well to P2MP TE LSPs.

The stateful nature of the PCE simplifies the information carried in PCEP messages, because an LSP can be referred to by a PCEP-specific LSP identifier, the PLSP-ID. This matters more for P2MP, where the messages are much larger. With a stateless PCE, a request to modify an existing tree has to present all the leaves and all the path information in the PCEP messages. With a stateful PCE, the messages can use the PLSP-ID to stand for everything about the LSP that has already been exchanged, and only the modifications need to be encoded, such as new or removed leaf nodes. The PLSP-ID is an index into the LSP database at the PCE and identifies the LSP at the PCC.

Where the placement of P2MP TE LSPs has to change in response to application demands, it is useful to support dynamic creation and tear down of P2MP TE LSPs. A PCE triggering the creation of P2MP TE LSPs on demand fits into a controller-based network architecture, where the intelligence in the controller decides when and where to set up paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A stateful path computer remembers the trees it manages, so each one has a short identifier. A message about a tree then only has to carry what changed, for example one branch that was added, instead of the whole tree with all its branches and paths. That is a large saving on a tree with many leaves, and it is the main reason this extension exists.

sections.title: The Functions a Stateful PCE Needs
sections.content:
The functions that RFC 8231 defines for a stateful PCE can be started either by a client towards a PCE or by a PCE towards a client. This document extends them to P2MP TE LSPs.

  • Capability advertisement, in both directions: the client and the PCE must both announce during PCEP session establishment that they support the stateful extensions for P2MP.
  • LSP state synchronization, from client to PCE: after the session is up, the PCE must learn the state of the client's P2MP TE LSPs before it can compute paths or change LSP attributes.
  • LSP update request, from PCE to client: the PCE asks for attributes of the client's P2MP TE LSPs to be changed.
  • LSP state report, from client to PCE: the client reports a change in the state of a P2MP TE LSP.
  • LSP control delegation, in both directions: the client grants the PCE the right to update the attributes of one or more P2MP TE LSPs, and the PCE becomes the authoritative source of those attributes for as long as the delegation lasts. The client may withdraw the delegation, or the PCE may give it up, at any time.
  • PCE-initiated LSP instantiation, from PCE to client: the PCE sends an LSP initiate message to set up or delete a P2MP TE LSP.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists what the two ends have to be able to do: say during session setup that they support trees, exchange the state of the trees, ask for changes to them, hand over control of a tree, and set a tree up or tear it down on request. Each of these is a separate exchange between the client and the path computer.

sections.title: Advertising the Capability
sections.content:
During the PCEP initialization phase, PCEP speakers advertise the stateful capability with the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV in the OPEN object. This document adds three flags to that TLV.

The N flag, the P2MP-CAPABILITY flag, means that the client is willing to send P2MP LSP state reports whenever the parameters or operational status of the tree change, and that the PCE wants to receive those reports. Both ends must advertise it for the P2MP extension of the PCRpt message to be allowed on a session. The M flag, the P2MP-LSP-UPDATE-CAPABILITY flag, means that the client allows its P2MP LSP parameters to be modified and that the PCE is able to update them. Both ends must advertise it for the P2MP extension of the PCUpd message. The P flag, the P2MP-LSP-INSTANTIATION-CAPABILITY flag, means that the client allows a PCE to instantiate a P2MP LSP and that the PCE supports doing so. Both ends must set it for PCE-initiated P2MP instantiation.

A PCEP speaker should still advertise the basic P2MP capability by the mechanisms of RFC 8306.

When the client and the PCEs are routers taking part in the same IGP, PCE discovery can use IGP advertisements, with the extensions for OSPF and IS-IS defined in RFC 5088 and RFC 5089. The optional PCE-CAP-FLAGS sub-TLV, of type 5, carries an array of 32-bit flag units in which each bit is one PCE capability. This document defines bit 13 for an active stateful PCE with P2MP, bit 14 for a passive stateful PCE with P2MP and bit 15 for PCE initiation with P2MP. A speaker that wants to use stateful PCEP for P2MP TE LSPs must still advertise the capability during PCEP session setup, and a client may start doing that even if it received no IGP capability advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anything else, the two ends have to say that they support trees. Each says so with a flag in the capability TLV of the session setup message: one flag for reporting tree state, one for changing a tree, and one for letting the path computer create a tree. The same capabilities can also be advertised in the routing protocol, so that a client can find path computers in the first place, but the session-level advertisement is what counts.

sections.title: Reporting the State of a Tree
sections.content:
The PCRpt message reports the current state of a path, and this document extends it to report the status of P2MP TE LSPs. Each P2MP TE LSP state report in a PCRpt message carries the actual P2MP TE LSP path attributes and the LSP status, and it is also used to delegate or revoke control of a P2MP TE LSP.

The P2MP END-POINTS object is mandatory for specifying the address of the P2MP leaves, grouped by leaf type. Leaf type 1 is for new leaves to add, leaf type 2 for old leaves to remove, leaf type 3 for old leaves whose path can be modified or reoptimized, and leaf type 4 for old leaves whose path must be left unchanged. When the status of a P2MP TE LSP is reported, the destinations must be grouped in the END-POINTS object by operational status and leaf type, so that leaves of the same type with the same status can be grouped together. Leaf type 3 is used for delegated P2MP TE LSPs and leaf type 4 for non-delegated ones. Configuration changes on a delegated tree are reported through a PCRpt message, with leaf type 1 for added leaves and leaf type 2 for removed ones.

The S2LS object must be carried in a PCRpt message along with the END-POINTS object when the N flag is set in the LSP object. If the S2LS object is missing, the receiving PCE must send a PCEP error message with Error-type 6, mandatory object missing, and Error-value 13, S2LS object missing. If the END-POINTS object is missing, it must send Error-type 6 with Error-value 3, END-POINTS object missing. At least one END-POINTS object must be present in the message for a P2MP LSP, which keeps compatibility with the point-to-point definition of a state report. During state synchronization, the PCRpt message reports the status of the full tree.
sections.plainLanguage: The client reports the state of a tree with a PCRpt message. The leaves are grouped by what is happening to them: newly added, removed, to be recomputed, or left as they are. A second object, the S2LS object, says whether each group of leaves is up or down. If that object is missing, the path computer rejects the report with an error.

sections.title: The New Objects and Flags
sections.content:
The LSP object of RFC 8231 carries the PLSP-ID that uniquely identifies an LSP for the life of a PCEP session, and the same identifier uniquely identifies a P2MP TE LSP. This document adds three flags to that object. The N flag means the message is for a P2MP TE LSP. The F flag means the LSP is fragmented and this is not the last piece, so the receiver waits for more fragments until it receives an LSP with the same PLSP-ID and the F bit clear. The E flag means the route is in compressed form, using Secondary Explicit Route and Secondary Record Route objects. These flags are used in PCRpt, PCUpd and PCInitiate messages; in PCReq and PCRep messages they have no meaning and must be ignored.

Two P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLVs are defined for the LSP object, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6. The P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV must be included in the LSP object in a PCRpt message for P2MP TE LSPs. If the N bit is set in the LSP object but the TLV is absent, the PCE must respond with error-type 6 and error-value 14, P2MP-LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV missing, and close the PCEP session. The TLV may be included in the LSP object of a PCUpd message, where the value of all zeros refers to all paths of a particular PLSP-ID. It should not be used in a PCInitiate message, because those identifiers are generated by the client on receipt of the message and reported back in a PCRpt message.

The IPv4 form has type 32 and a fixed length of 16 octets, holding the IPv4 tunnel sender address, a 16-bit LSP ID, a 16-bit Tunnel ID, a 32-bit Extended Tunnel ID and a 32-bit P2MP ID. The IPv6 form has type 33 and a fixed length of 40 octets, with the same fields except that the tunnel sender address is 128 bits and the Extended Tunnel ID is 128 bits.

The S2LS object, for Source-to-Leaves, reports the state of one or more destinations encoded in the END-POINTS object. Its Object-Class is 41 and its Object-Type is 1. Its flag field holds the O field, an operational status of 3 bits for the group of destinations, with the same values as the Operational field in the LSP object. The unassigned bits must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt. When the N flag is set, the O field in the LSP object is the status of the whole tree and the O field in the S2LS object is the status of one group of destinations. If the two conflict, for example the tree is down while a group is up, the speaker must raise an error with error-type 10, reception of an invalid object, and error-value 22, mismatch of O field in S2LS and LSP object.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things identify and describe a tree in the messages: a flag in the LSP object that says the message is about a tree, a TLV that carries the tunnel and tree identifiers, and the S2LS object that carries the status of a group of leaves. The identifiers are 16 octets long for IPv4 and 40 octets for IPv6.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Refusals
sections.content:
The total length of a PCEP message, including the common header, is (2^16)-1 bytes. In some scenarios a P2MP report or update request does not fit into one message, for example the initial report for a large tree. The F flag in the LSP object signals that the report, update or initiate request was too large and has been split across several messages. All the messages of one series use the same PLSP-ID, so the receiver can tell that they belong together; for a series of PCInitiate messages the PLSP-ID is 0 and the SRP-ID-number is also the same.

For a fragmented report, every message except the last has the F flag set. If the PCE never receives the last part, it reports error-type 18, P2MP fragmentation error, with error-value 2, fragmented report failure. The same error-type is used for an update, where error-value 3 is fragmented update failure, and for an initiation, where error-value 4 is fragmented instantiation failure.

The extensions in this document must not be used if the PCE did not advertise the stateful capability with P2MP. If the client understands the N and M flags but did not advertise the capability, then on receipt of a PCUpd message it should raise an error with error-type 19, invalid operation, and error-value 12, and terminate the PCEP session. If the PCE understands the N flag but did not advertise the capability, then on receipt of a PCRpt message it should raise error-type 19 with error-value 11 and terminate the session. The same rule applies to PCE-initiated trees, with error-value 13 for an instantiation request that was not advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: A big tree can need more than one message. The F flag marks the pieces except the last, and the receiver puts them back together using the tree identifier. If a piece never arrives, the error code says which kind of message was incomplete. The RFC also says what to do when one end uses these messages without having advertised the capability: report an error and close the session.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateful operations on P2MP TE LSPs use more processor time and more bandwidth on the wire than the same operations on point-to-point LSPs. If a rogue client could request unauthorized stateful operations, it could mount a denial-of-service attack against a PCE, which would disrupt the network and deny service to other clients. Similarly, an attacker could flood a client with PCUpd messages at a rate that exceeds either the client's ability to process them or the network's ability to signal the changes, by spoofing messages or by compromising the PCE itself.

The RFC therefore lists the requirements that apply. It is recommended that these PCEP extensions only be activated on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs belonging to the same administrative authority, using Transport Layer Security as described in the recommendations of RFC 7525. The security considerations for path computation requests and responses are those of RFC 8306, and the considerations for stateful operations such as state report, synchronization, delegation and update are those of RFC 8231. The sections of RFC 5440 on security continue to apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Trees make the signalling heavier, so a client that is not allowed to send it could overload the path computer and hurt everyone else. The RFC therefore says to run these sessions over an authenticated and encrypted connection between systems under the same administration.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Code point 32 for the IPv4 form; the IPv6 form is type 33.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Fixed value of 16 octets for the value that follows.

fields.name: IPv4 Tunnel Sender Address
fields.desc: The IPv4 address of the node that sends the tunnel.

fields.name: Tunnel ID
fields.desc: The 16-bit Tunnel ID identifier, constant over the life of the tunnel.

fields.name: P2MP ID
fields.desc: The 32-bit P2MP ID identifier of the point-to-multipoint LSP.
